cycle1_result: 162/184 (88.0%) referred for VFC review; 98.1% reached afterwards (3 patients, 1.9%, not reached); 29/162 (17.9%) discharged 'virtually'; 137/291 (45.0%) appointments remote. Median total ED time 95 minutes vs 131 minutes at baseline (p<0.001).

cycle1_result: No designated MBD lead in 39% of centres (33/84); inadequate radiographs in 19% (160/846); no up-to-date staging CT in 29% (247/846); oncology opinion 69% (584/846); prognosis estimation 38% (223/846).

title: Orthopaedic Out of Bed Project (OOBP): improving early mobilisation following femoral fracture using a therapy-led education programme.
standard: NHFD metric: patient mobilised (standing or hoisted) out of bed by the day after surgery; target at least the UK national average of 81%
finding: Mean 60% of patients mobilised by the day after surgery. Hip Sprint cohort (n=60): 1.7% mobilised by healthcare assistants before physiotherapy assessment.
change: Therapy-led ward education programme for trauma healthcare assistants (1-hour 2:1 face-to-face session plus observed sign-off), ward posters and Trust media campaign, delivered over two PDSA cycles (June-July 2020 and June-August 2022)
setting: 35-bed trauma ward, James Paget University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (district general hospital), Great Yarmouth
cycle1_period: 6 months before the intervention (2019/2020, NHFD data); Hip Sprint audit September and December 2019
cycle1_result: Mean 60% of patients mobilised by the day after surgery. Hip Sprint cohort (n=60): 1.7% mobilised by healthcare assistants before physiotherapy assessment.
intervention: Therapy-led ward education programme for trauma healthcare assistants (1-hour 2:1 face-to-face session plus observed sign-off), ward posters and Trust media campaign, delivered over two PDSA cycles (June-July 2020 and June-August 2022)
cycle2_result: Mean 79.2% mobilised by the day after surgery after PDSA cycle 2 (from 60% in 2019). Healthcare assistant mobilisation before physiotherapy assessment 30% (n=51 cohort).
other_findings: After PDSA cycle 1 the rate rose to a mean of 78% but fell back to 71.8% in 2021, attributed to staff turnover. 30-day mortality fell from 10.1% to 7% between 2019 and 2022 (causality not established).
authors: Gray R; Taylor M; Bullock R
citation: Gray R, Taylor M, Bullock R. Orthopaedic Out of Bed Project (OOBP): improving early mobilisation following femoral fracture using a therapy-led education programme. BMJ Open Qual. 2023;12(Suppl 2):e002301. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2023-002301. PMID: 37783518.

title: An Audit on the Pre-operative Fasting Time of Trauma-List Orthopaedic Patients at a District General Hospital in Chichester, United Kingdom.
standard: RCN, AAGBI, European Society of Anaesthesiology and ASA guidelines: fasting of two hours for clear fluids and six hours for solids
finding: All 50 patients (100%) fasted beyond six hours for solids (mean 15.8 hours, range 9–24) and 49 (98%) beyond two hours for clear fluids (mean 10.5 hours, range 2–20); only 5 (10%) had correct documented fasting instructions; 31 (62%) were 'nil by mouth from midnight'.
setting: Orthopaedic trauma list, St Richard's Hospital, district general hospital, Chichester
cycle1_result: All 50 patients (100%) fasted beyond six hours for solids (mean 15.8 hours, range 9–24) and 49 (98%) beyond two hours for clear fluids (mean 10.5 hours, range 2–20); only 5 (10%) had correct documented fasting instructions; 31 (62%) were 'nil by mouth from midnight'.
intervention: not reported
cycle2_result: not reported
other_findings: Staff survey showed poor knowledge: only 42.9% of ward nurses knew the 6 hour/2 hour rule. Only 52% received preoperative IV fluids; a 'sip till send' policy has since been introduced.
authors: Perera H; Wusu A; Mohammad A; Qulaghassi MZ; Abdulkarim A

title: Audit on the Adequacy of Consenting Practices for Neck of Femur Fracture Surgeries.

finding: Infection documented in 98.4%, blood clots 95.2%, bleeding 92.1%, neurovascular injury 79.4%, dislocation 77.8%, pain 74.6%, anaesthetic complications 73%, failure 68.3%, leg length discrepancy 60.3%, bone damage/fracture 50.8%, death 49.2%, wound complications 42.9%, hip stiffness 14.3%, catheterisation 0%. setting: St Richard's Hospital, Chichester; district general hospital trauma and orthopaedic department
cycle1_result: Infection documented in 98.4%, blood clots 95.2%, bleeding 92.1%, neurovascular injury 79.4%, dislocation 77.8%, pain 74.6%, anaesthetic complications 73%, failure 68.3%, leg length discrepancy 60.3%, bone damage/fracture 50.8%, death 49.2%, wound complications 42.9%, hip stiffness 14.3%, catheterisation 0%. Diagnosis missing in 22.2% (n=14), benefits in 12.7% (n=8), responsible consultant in 28.6% (n=18), blood transfusion in 25.4% (n=16).

topic: Hip fracture and registry data quality
title: Development of a New Knee Arthroscopy Operative Proforma Saving Thousands of British Pounds.
standard: Correct ICD-10 and OPCS-4 coding of arthroscopic knee procedures from the operation note; proforma based on Royal College guidance for operation notes
finding: 17/34 (50%) cases coded incorrectly; tariff value £85,026 as coded versus £114,351 after correction, a loss of £29,325.
change: New coding-friendly knee arthroscopy operation note proforma with tick boxes, developed with coding staff and agreed at a consensus meeting, disseminated by email, notice boards and governance meetings.
setting: Two centres of one trauma and orthopaedic service (Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust / North Manchester General Hospital), knee arthroscopy day cases
cycle1_result: 17/34 (50%) cases coded incorrectly; tariff value £85,026 as coded versus £114,351 after correction, a loss of £29,325.
intervention: New coding-friendly knee arthroscopy operation note proforma with tick boxes, developed with coding staff and agreed at a consensus meeting, disseminated by email, notice boards and governance meetings.
cycle2_result: 2/37 (5%) cases coded incorrectly; £86,886 as coded versus £89,540 after correction, a loss of £2654.
other_findings: Most coding errors came from vague documentation of preoperative diagnoses and additional procedures (e.g. extra meniscectomy or cartilage debridement). Uptake of the proforma was slow and some cases were excluded for incorrect use of the form.

title: A Clinical Audit of Orthopaedic Clinical Documentation of Acute Ankle Fractures: A Quality Improvement Project.
standard: BOAST ankle fracture standards and NICE NG37: documentation of mechanism, skin integrity, circulation, neurological examination and repeat neurovascular examination after reduction; target 100%
finding: Mechanism of injury 86%; skin integrity 54%; circulation status 54%; detailed vascular examination 17%; neurological examination 54%; sensory detail 48%; MRC motor scale 48%; repeat neurovascular examination after reduction 56%; overall precise documentation of clinical findings 17%.
change: Targeted education on documentation standards at induction and trauma meetings, with case-based discussion reports; made a permanent part of departmental teaching.
setting: Trauma and orthopaedics, single centre (audit approved at University Hospitals Dorset, Poole General Hospital; authors at Dorset County Hospital)
cycle1_result: Mechanism of injury 86%; skin integrity 54%; circulation status 54%; detailed vascular examination 17%; neurological examination 54%; sensory detail 48%; MRC motor scale 48%; repeat neurovascular examination after reduction 56%; overall precise documentation of clinical findings 17%.
intervention: Targeted education on documentation standards at induction and trauma meetings, with case-based discussion reports; made a permanent part of departmental teaching.

topic: Suspected cauda equina time to MRI
title: Suspected Cauda Equina Syndrome: Can the Presence of an Orthopaedic Doctor in the Emergency Department Reduce Waiting Times for MRI Scans and Inpatient Stays?
standard: NICE, BASS and SBNS guidelines and local trust protocol; National Suspected CES Pathway recommends MRI within four hours of request
finding: Mean MRI waiting time 12.5 hours (8am-4pm 9.5 h; 4pm-12am 18 h; 12am-8am 8.5 h); same-day discharge 27 (29%); inpatient stay 66 (71%)
change: Introduction of a middle-grade trauma and orthopaedic doctor in the emergency department (urgent treatment centre) to assess suspected CES patients
setting: Wythenshawe Hospital, Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, a district general hospital with no on-site spinal services; trauma and orthopaedic referrals from the emergency department
cycle1_result: Mean MRI waiting time 12.5 hours (8am-4pm 9.5 h; 4pm-12am 18 h; 12am-8am 8.5 h); same-day discharge 27 (29%); inpatient stay 66 (71%)
intervention: Introduction of a middle-grade trauma and orthopaedic doctor in the emergency department (urgent treatment centre) to assess suspected CES patients
cycle2_result: Mean MRI waiting time 8 hours (8am-4pm 5.5 h; 4pm-12am 13 h; 12am-8am 6.5 h); all MRI scans and reports within 24 hours; same-day discharge 21 (58%); inpatient stay 15 (42%)

title: Improving Completion Rates of Treatment Escalation Plan (TEP) in a London Teaching Hospital: A Quality Improvement Study.
standard: Trust treatment escalation plan (TEP) policy: TEP completed for emergency adult admissions, within 48 hours
finding: Overall TEP completion 69.5%; completed within 48 hours 47.82%; mean time to complete 4.4 days; mean overrides 3.2; longest 35 days; 24 instances of skipping. Incomplete TEPs 30.4% (n=7).
change: Revised local TEP pathway/algorithm allowing F1+ doctors to complete TEPs for young patients with simple fractures, algorithm displayed in trauma room, emails, individual teaching, and reminders to discuss TEP status on the post-take ward round.
setting: Orthopaedic wards, University Hospital Lewisham (London teaching hospital), adult inpatients
cycle1_result: Overall TEP completion 69.5%; completed within 48 hours 47.82%; mean time to complete 4.4 days; mean overrides 3.2; longest 35 days; 24 instances of skipping. Incomplete TEPs 30.4% (n=7).
intervention: Revised local TEP pathway/algorithm allowing F1+ doctors to complete TEPs for young patients with simple fractures, algorithm displayed in trauma room, emails, individual teaching, and reminders to discuss TEP status on the post-take ward round.
cycle2_result: Overall completion 88.2%; completed within 48 hours 35.29%; mean time 3.7 days; mean overrides 1.3; longest 13 days; 5 instances of skipping. Incomplete TEPs 11.76% (n=2).

topic: Elective cancellations due to asymptomatic bacteriuria
title: Introduction of a New Protocol to Limit the Number of Cancelled Elective Orthopaedic Operations Due to Asymptomatic Bacteriuria.
finding: Of 33 all-cause cancellations, 7 (21.2%) were cancelled for UTI risk on positive urinalysis; only 1 (14.3%) of these was symptomatic, so 6 (85.7%) were cancelled for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
change: New symptom-based protocol from 1 May 2019: all patients complete a 7-item UTI symptom questionnaire and surgery is cancelled only if two or more symptoms are reported, regardless of urinalysis.
setting: Lister Hospital, Stevenage (East & North Herts NHS Trust), large district general hospital offering tertiary orthopaedic services; cancelled elective orthopaedic operations
cycle1_result: Of 33 all-cause cancellations, 7 (21.2%) were cancelled for UTI risk on positive urinalysis; only 1 (14.3%) of these was symptomatic, so 6 (85.7%) were cancelled for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
intervention: New symptom-based protocol from 1 May 2019: all patients complete a 7-item UTI symptom questionnaire and surgery is cancelled only if two or more symptoms are reported, regardless of urinalysis.
cycle2_result: Of 45 all-cause cancellations, 2 (4.4%) were cancelled for UTI risk, both symptomatic; 4 (8.8%) had positive urinalysis, the 2 asymptomatic ones cancelled for unrelated reasons. No cancellations for asymptomatic bacteriuria; estimated 71.4% reduction in cancellations for UTI risk.
other_findings: Patients with positive urinalysis whose operations were not cancelled were not captured, so the true effect is estimated. Each cancelled operation was estimated to waste 2.1 hours of theatre time (about £2,525).
authors: Taylor N; Jaques A; Antar M; Raghu A; Tai S
citation: Taylor N, Jaques A, Antar M, Raghu A, Tai S. Introduction of a New Protocol to Limit the Number of Cancelled Elective Orthopaedic Operations Due to Asymptomatic Bacteriuria. Cureus. 2023;15(12):e51097. doi:10.7759/cureus.51097. PMID: 38274927.

topic: Paediatric buckle and forearm fracture management
title: Clinical Audit of Manipulation of Paediatric Forearm Fractures in the Emergency Department at a District General Hospital: A Quality Improvement Project.
standard: BOAST and GIRFT recommendations that units have protocols for manipulation of paediatric forearm fractures under procedural analgesia in the ED, avoiding admission and general anaesthesia; local standard operating procedure
finding: Pre-implementation (n=11 suitable fractures): manipulation in ED 1 (9.1%); theatre required 4 (36.4%).
change: New standard operating procedure and paediatric fracture manipulation pathway in the ED using intranasal fentanyl and Entonox, agreed with ED, orthopaedics, radiology and theatre managers; information leaflets planned after cycle 2.
setting: Poole Hospital, University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust, district general hospital emergency department and trauma and orthopaedics
cycle1_result: Pre-implementation (n=11 suitable fractures): manipulation in ED 1 (9.1%); theatre required 4 (36.4%).
intervention: New standard operating procedure and paediatric fracture manipulation pathway in the ED using intranasal fentanyl and Entonox, agreed with ED, orthopaedics, radiology and theatre managers; information leaflets planned after cycle 2.
cycle2_result: Third cycle (n=52): manipulation in ED 9 (17.3%); theatre required 1 (1.9%). All nine manipulable fractures were manipulated in the ED.
other_findings: Second cycle (n=74): manipulation in ED 11 (14.9%), theatre required 21 (28.4%); 27% of manipulable fractures were manipulated in ED and none of these later needed theatre. title: Improving the Safety of Tourniquet Use in a Trauma Theatre According to the British Orthopaedic Association Guidelines: A Closed Loop Audit.
standard: BOAST guidance on the safe use of intraoperative tourniquets (2021): document skin condition and isolation method, pressure SBP + 50-100 mmHg upper limb and + 70-130 mmHg lower limb in adults, ischaemic time under 120 minutes
finding: Skin status documented 37%; isolation method documented 43%; tourniquet pressure documented 71%; pressure within BOAST safe limit 25%; tourniquet time under 120 minutes in 97%.
change: Results presented at departmental audit meeting; tourniquet details made a mandatory part of the electronic operation note template; labels on tourniquet machines to calculate pressure; BOAST guidance posted in the theatre doctors' office.
setting: Trauma theatre, Trauma and Orthopaedic Department of a district general hospital (Russells Hall Hospital, Dudley)
cycle1_result: Skin status documented 37%; isolation method documented 43%; tourniquet pressure documented 71%; pressure within BOAST safe limit 25%; tourniquet time under 120 minutes in 97%.
intervention: Results presented at departmental audit meeting; tourniquet details made a mandatory part of the electronic operation note template; labels on tourniquet machines to calculate pressure; BOAST guidance posted in the theatre doctors' office.
cycle2_result: Skin status documented 69% (p = 0.004); isolation method 74% (p = 0.003); pressure documented 94% (p = 0.003); pressure within BOAST safe limit 75%; tourniquet time under 120 minutes in 97%.
other_findings: Mean pressure above SBP fell from 125.9 to 99.9 mmHg (upper limb) and 154.2 to 121.7 mmHg (lower limb); about 25% still used pressures above the recommended range and surgeons not using the template still omitted details.

title: Introducing a new proforma for the safe use of intraoperative tourniquets in orthopaedic surgery.
standard: BOAST 'The Safe Use of Intraoperative Tourniquets': document exsanguination method, isolation method, skin condition, pressure and duration; pressure lower limb SBP + 70–130 mmHg, upper limb SBP + 50–100 mmHg; duration ideally < 120 min
finding: Exsanguination method documented 5.6%, isolation (shut-off drape) 2.4%, skin condition 0%; duration not in operative note 23.0%, not recorded at all 1.6%; > 120 min in 1.6%; pressure within standard in 24.3% lower limb, 34.8% upper limb and 66.7% paediatric cases.
change: Local presentation at trust Quality & Safety Half Day and 'PRESSURE' mnemonic posters in theatres and offices, followed by a new electronic patient record with a tourniquet section and BOAST-based auto-text proforma in the operation note.
setting: Ashford and St Peter's Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust; trauma and elective orthopaedic surgery across both sites
cycle1_result: Exsanguination method documented 5.6%, isolation (shut-off drape) 2.4%, skin condition 0%; duration not in operative note 23.0%, not recorded at all 1.6%; > 120 min in 1.6%; pressure within standard in 24.3% lower limb, 34.8% upper limb and 66.7% paediatric cases.
intervention: Local presentation at trust Quality & Safety Half Day and 'PRESSURE' mnemonic posters in theatres and offices, followed by a new electronic patient record with a tourniquet section and BOAST-based auto-text proforma in the operation note.
cycle2_result: Exsanguination method documented 42.9% (p = 0.001), isolation 42.9% (p = 0.0001), skin condition 64.3% (p = 0.0001); duration not in operative note 10.2% (p = 0.0269), not recorded 0%; none > 120 min; pressure within standard 13.0% lower limb, 35.7% upper limb, 14.2% paediatric (no significant change).
other_findings: An interim re-audit in March 2022 after education alone (n = 153) showed little change (e.g. exsanguination 9.8%, skin condition 5.2%). Staff survey (n = 19) found over 50% sized tourniquets on 'whatever looks the best fit' and 31.6% did not know paediatric pressures.

title: A Quality Improvement Project to Measure and Improve the Quality of Below-Knee Ankle Cast Application in Emergency Departments.
standard: AO Foundation guidance: ankle immobilised in neutral plantigrade position; acceptable tibia-to-sole angle 80-100 degrees on lateral radiograph
finding: Mean angle 108.5 degrees (SD 11.7); 18/65 (27.7%) within 80-100 degrees (DGH 1 n=32, DGH 2 n=33).
change: Single interactive session led by plaster technicians (for UTC nurses at DGH 1 and for ED junior doctors at DGH 2) plus educational posters where plastering occurred.
setting: Urgent treatment centre and emergency departments of two district general hospitals
cycle1_result: Mean angle 108.5 degrees (SD 11.7); 18/65 (27.7%) within 80-100 degrees (DGH 1 n=32, DGH 2 n=33).
intervention: Single interactive session led by plaster technicians (for UTC nurses at DGH 1 and for ED junior doctors at DGH 2) plus educational posters where plastering occurred.

cycle1_result: 22/44 (50.0%) referrals without an indication were given or advised antibiotics; 10/84 (12%) with an indication were neither given nor advised antibiotics.

cycle1_result: 39% of non-operative patients triaged to the VFC within 24 hours; 61% sent directly to face-to-face clinic. 35,399 face-to-face fracture clinic appointments (also given as 35,339 in the results).

title: Improving Orthostatic Hypotension Screening in Fall Prevention: A Two-Cycle Audit on Falls Assessment and Lying and Standing Blood Pressure Measurement.
standard: NICE falls guidance: completion of falls assessment and lying and standing blood pressure measurement; target 100%
finding: Falls assessment completed 38/41 (93%); lying and standing BP recorded 14/41 (34%).
change: Cycle 1 results presented at departmental teaching, daily reminders at the morning huddle, educational flyers and targeted education for doctors, nurses and healthcare staff.
setting: Orthopaedic rehabilitation ward, district general hospital in North East England
cycle1_result: Falls assessment completed 38/41 (93%); lying and standing BP recorded 14/41 (34%).

cycle2_result: Falls assessment completed 40/41 (98%) (p = 0.61); lying and standing BP recorded 28/41 (68%) (p = 0.004).
other_findings: Systolic drop of 20 mmHg or more found in 5/14 (36%) then 13/28 (46.4%) of those measured. LSBP was sometimes marked as completed in the falls assessment when it was not done.

topic: Image transfer time for neurosurgical referrals
title: Assessment of urgent investigative images transfer effectiveness from trauma and orthopaedic to neurosurgery department: a quality improvement project.
standard: 100% of NORSe referrals should have images sent to neurosurgery within 1 hour; neurosurgery should review imaging and respond within 6 hours at least 90% of the time
finding: Mean time from referral to image transfer 18 hours; 36% (n=14) transferred within 1 hour; neurosurgery response averaged 18 hours with 38% (n=14) reviewed within 6 hours.
change: Image exchange portal software introduced so T&O registrars, then junior doctors, could send images directly without the PACS team; supported by departmental presentation, video demonstration, emailed instructions, QR-code posters and induction teaching.
setting: Trauma and orthopaedics department, Sandwell and West Birmingham Hospitals NHS Trust, referring to Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham neurosurgery
cycle1_result: Mean time from referral to image transfer 18 hours; 36% (n=14) transferred within 1 hour; neurosurgery response averaged 18 hours with 38% (n=14) reviewed within 6 hours.
intervention: Image exchange portal software introduced so T&O registrars, then junior doctors, could send images directly without the PACS team; supported by departmental presentation, video demonstration, emailed instructions, QR-code posters and induction teaching.
cycle2_result: Mean time to image transfer 3.6 hours; 61% (n=96) transferred within 1 hour; neurosurgery response averaged 7 hours with 87% (n=138) reviewed within 6 hours; 45% (71) of images sent by the T&O team.
other_findings: Intermediate cycle (March to May 2024, n=64): mean transfer 9.3 hours, 28% within 1 hour, 43% reviewed within 6 hours, and only 6.2% of images sent by T&O owing to poor registrar uptake. Neither target was fully met; the abstract quotes 59% within 1 hour.
authors: Khan M; Khaleeq T; Theivendran K
citation: Khan M, Khaleeq T, Theivendran K. Assessment of urgent investigative images transfer effectiveness from trauma and orthopaedic to neurosurgery department: a quality improvement project. BMJ Open Qual. 2025;14(2):e003126. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2024-003126. PMID: 40345702.

topic: Suspected cauda equina time to MRI
title: Improving the suspected cauda equina syndrome pathway at a district general hospital: a quality improvement project.
standard: GIRFT National Suspected CES Pathway 2023: emergency MRI within 4 hours of request; local SMART aim of median under 4 hours from ED attendance to MRI within 1 year
finding: Median time from ED presentation to MRI 5.9 hours (IQR 4.9–14.7) although median MRI request to scan was 1.7 hours (IQR 1.1–3.7), meeting the GIRFT target; 8% of patients incorrectly sent to the GP-led MEDOCC service. At PDSA 1: 38% of MRIs unnecessary, 0.5 CES MRIs/day, time to analgesia 5.3 hours (IQR 3.8–7.0), 9% inappropriately triaged to MEDOCC.
change: Three PDSA cycles (July 2023 to January 2024): CES working group and trust-level awareness; new locally adapted SOP based on the GIRFT pathway with CES-specific shorter MRI sequences; ED triage and assessment posters, board round, grand round and senior-led teaching. Planned extension of MRI hours was not achieved.
setting: Medway Maritime Hospital, Gillingham; district general hospital emergency department without on-site emergency spinal surgery
cycle1_result: Median time from ED presentation to MRI 5.9 hours (IQR 4.9–14.7) although median MRI request to scan was 1.7 hours (IQR 1.1–3.7), meeting the GIRFT target; 8% of patients incorrectly sent to the GP-led MEDOCC service. At PDSA 1: 38% of MRIs unnecessary, 0.5 CES MRIs/day, time to analgesia 5.3 hours (IQR 3.8–7.0), 9% inappropriately triaged to MEDOCC.
intervention: Three PDSA cycles (July 2023 to January 2024): CES working group and trust-level awareness; new locally adapted SOP based on the GIRFT pathway with CES-specific shorter MRI sequences; ED triage and assessment posters, board round, grand round and senior-led teaching. Planned extension of MRI hours was not achieved.
cycle2_period: PDSA 3, cycles run July 2023 to January 2024
cycle2_result: Approximately 27 patients per cycle. Median ED presentation to MRI 5.7 hours (IQR 4.1–14.3), primary aim not met; GIRFT 4-hour request-to-scan target met in all cycles. Unnecessary MRIs fell from 38% to 18%, CES MRIs 0.5/day to 0.4/day, time to analgesia 5.3 to 4.2 hours (IQR 2.7–7.0), and inappropriate MEDOCC referrals 9% to 0%.
other_findings: Time to MRI rose to 9.9 hours in PDSA 2 amid ED pressures and industrial action; 43/81 patients presented at times making same-day MRI unlikely because scanners ran only until 20:00, and by PDSA 3 attendance to MRI request was still a median 3.9 hours.
authors: Conte A; Lingham A; Nagulendran S; Chaudhary U; Alsayeh S; Malkania B; Sharma S; Watts P; Mitchell M; Davis A; Mueller M
citation: Conte A, Lingham A, Nagulendran S, Chaudhary U, Alsayeh S, Malkania B, et al.. Improving the suspected cauda equina syndrome pathway at a district general hospital: a quality improvement project. BMJ Open Qual. 2025;14(2):e003081. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2024-003081. PMID: 40441733.

finding: Overall abutment fracture rate 0.6% (105/17,207), 1.6% below the 2.2% literature rate and 1.2% below the 1.8% Ankylos rate; first molar fracture rate 1.9% (87/4,709)
setting: Specialist dental implant practice (private practice)
cycle1_result: Overall abutment fracture rate 0.6% (105/17,207), 1.6% below the 2.2% literature rate and 1.2% below the 1.8% Ankylos rate; first molar fracture rate 1.9% (87/4,709)

topic: Ottawa rules and radiograph request appropriateness
title: Assessing Compliance With Ottawa Foot and Ankle Rules in the Emergency Department: A Closed-Loop Quality Improvement Project.
standard: ED clerking documentation and X-ray request clinical details should contain the relevant Ottawa Ankle or Foot Rule criteria in all cases (NICE; RCR/IR(ME)R 2017)
finding: 100 ankle and 100 foot X-ray requests. Ankle: documentation compliance 74%, X-ray request compliance 43%. Foot: documentation compliance 48%, X-ray request compliance 32%.
change: First-cycle results distributed and an Ottawa rules handout given to ED staff, plus a small-group teaching session for ED junior doctors on assessing, documenting and requesting foot and ankle X-rays (mid-April 2024)
setting: Emergency department, South London district general hospital
cycle1_result: 100 ankle and 100 foot X-ray requests. Ankle: documentation compliance 74%, X-ray request compliance 43%. Foot: documentation compliance 48%, X-ray request compliance 32%.
intervention: First-cycle results distributed and an Ottawa rules handout given to ED staff, plus a small-group teaching session for ED junior doctors on assessing, documenting and requesting foot and ankle X-rays (mid-April 2024)
cycle2_result: Ankle: documentation 87% (p<.05), X-ray request 57% (p<.05). Foot: documentation 78% (p<.001 in abstract; p<.0001 in results), X-ray request 54% (p<.01).
other_findings: Ankle fracture rate rose from 17% to 22% (p=.37) and midfoot fracture rate stayed at 15%. Foot compliance stayed lower than ankle compliance in both cycles; authors suggest an electronic X-ray request template.

title: Improving Patient Care and Clinical Services: Compliance With the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Guidelines for Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis After Hip and Knee Arthroplasty.
standard: NICE VTE guidance: THR 28 days LMWH plus anti-embolism stockings until discharge; TKR 14 days LMWH plus stockings
finding: THR 23/25 (92%) and TKR 20/23 (87%) received enoxaparin plus stockings; overall compliance 90%.
change: Arthroplasty discharge pack displayed as posters and handouts at the arthroplasty station, regular teaching sessions on NICE discharge guidance, and final check of discharge letters by the nurse in charge.

cycle1_result: THR 23/25 (92%) and TKR 20/23 (87%) received enoxaparin plus stockings; overall compliance 90%.

cycle2_result: THR 24/24 (100%) and TKR 22/23 (96%) correct; overall compliance 98%.
other_findings: Overall compliance was calculated as the average of the THR and TKR rates; patient outcomes were not recorded.

title: Designing a new orthopaedic trauma meeting proforma to improve documentation in a large UK teaching hospital.
standard: Locally designed trauma meeting documentation standards (no UK guideline exists); record keeping guidance from GMC, RCS England and BMA
finding: 58/90 (64%) had some documentation. Consultant on call 43%, other consultants 29%, imaging 20%, MDT concerns 7%, diagnosis 29%, laterality 22%, clear plan 63%, weight-bearing 1%.
change: Electronic trauma meeting proforma (EPR shortcut) introduced, then revised after MDT feedback (theatre checklist added); teaching video and poster for new doctors before the one-year re-audit.
setting: Trauma and orthopaedic department, Wythenshawe Hospital, Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust (acute teaching hospital)
cycle1_result: 58/90 (64%) had some documentation. Consultant on call 43%, other consultants 29%, imaging 20%, MDT concerns 7%, diagnosis 29%, laterality 22%, clear plan 63%, weight-bearing 1%.
intervention: Electronic trauma meeting proforma (EPR shortcut) introduced, then revised after MDT feedback (theatre checklist added); teaching video and poster for new doctors before the one-year re-audit.
cycle2_result: 71/85 (84%) had some documentation. Consultant on call, other consultants and imaging 100%, diagnosis 97%, laterality 75%, clear plan 98%.

title: The impact of direct oral anticoagulants on hip fracture care in Australia and New Zealand: a prospective patient sprint audit.
standard: ANZ hip fracture clinical care standard and international consensus: surgery within 36 hours (including for patients on DOACs)
finding: Median time to surgery 39 h (IQR 24–48) on DOACs, 25 h (IQR 20–39) on no antithrombotic and 27 h (IQR 20–44) on other antithrombotics; DOAC patients had higher odds of surgery >36 h (aOR 3.65, 95% CI 2.40–5.55); 43% of DOAC patients had surgery within 36 h versus 61% on other antithrombotics.
setting: Sprint audit of 31 hospitals (24 Australia, 7 New Zealand) in the Australian and New Zealand Hip Fracture Registry; patients on DOACs versus other or no antithrombotics
cycle1_result: Median time to surgery 39 h (IQR 24–48) on DOACs, 25 h (IQR 20–39) on no antithrombotic and 27 h (IQR 20–44) on other antithrombotics; DOAC patients had higher odds of surgery >36 h (aOR 3.65, 95% CI 2.40–5.55); 43% of DOAC patients had surgery within 36 h versus 61% on other antithrombotics.
intervention: not reported
cycle2_result: not reported
other_findings: 18% (192) were on DOACs; transfusion rates did not differ (23% vs 17% vs 22%). Only 5/24 Australian and all 7 New Zealand hospitals had a DOAC protocol, and 73% restarted DOACs >48 h after surgery.

title: Post-operative Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis for Non-arthroplasty Knee Surgery: A Closed Loop Clinical Audit.

finding: Arthroscopy with anaesthetic time >90 minutes 2/4 (50%) received prophylaxis; other non-arthroplasty surgery 9/25 (36%).
change: Formal teaching session for the joint replacement unit team by a senior consultant on recording anaesthetic time, weight-bearing status and VTE prescription on operation notes and postoperative instructions.
setting: Joint replacement unit, tertiary orthopaedic hospital (University Hospitals Dorset / Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital affiliations); elective non-arthroplasty knee procedures
cycle1_result: Arthroscopy with anaesthetic time >90 minutes 2/4 (50%) received prophylaxis; other non-arthroplasty surgery 9/25 (36%).

cycle2_result: Arthroscopy >90 minutes 6/11 (55%) (p=1.0); other non-arthroplasty surgery 27/40 (68%) (p=0.02).
